paras: The lynching of Morely was the hanging, in early May 1888, of a man named Morely or Morley, 'said to be a half-breed', at or near Oak Ridge settlement, Mississippi, after he was accused of waylaying and shooting James Newbaker. The only account was a brief wire dispatch from Vicksburg, which said no particulars of the hanging had been learned. Newspapers from Georgia to Kansas reprinted it within about a week.

According to the dispatch, information reached Vicksburg on or about May 8 that James Newbaker of Oak Ridge settlement had been waylaid and shot, one of his ears being completely severed. The dispatch named his assailant as a man called Morely, 'said to be a half breed'. Morely was 'soon afterward lynched', but the report said nothing of who hanged him, how many took part, or whether he had been arrested first. No report gives Newbaker's race or the cause of the shooting.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage, and no follow-up on Newbaker's condition was found.

The Savannah Morning News printed the dispatch first, on May 9, under the headline 'Shooting Followed by Lynching'. On May 10 the Wheeling Register ran it as 'They Lynched His Assailant', the Wichita Eagle as 'Lynching of a Half-Breed', and the Springfield Daily Republic in Ohio under the heading 'A Wednesday Matinee in Mississippi'. A week later two Kansas weeklies, the Abilene Weekly Reflector and the Dodge City Times, carried a shortened text headed 'Lynched' that dropped the severed ear.

The Indiana State Sentinel reduced the story to one line in a column of miscellaneous news, saying Newbaker 'was assassinated by one Morley, who was lynched later'. None of these papers commented on the lynching, and the only racial description in any of them was the label 'half-breed', which the Wichita Eagle put in its headline.

The copies differ on dates: the Savannah version is dated May 8 and says the news arrived 'to-day', most others are dated May 9 and say 'yesterday', and the Springfield copy is dated May 10. The Sentinel's statement that Newbaker was assassinated is at odds with the fuller dispatch, which says only that he was shot and lost an ear.

reader.title: Lynching of Morely
bases: Every report says Newbaker's alleged assailant Morely was 'soon afterward lynched' and refers to 'his hanging' (A1, A2, A5).

The dispatch reports Morely was lynched by hanging after being named as Newbaker's assailant, which supports an illegal killing in retaliation for an alleged crime (A1, A2, A5). No report describes who hanged him or how many took part, so a group of three or more is implied by the word 'lynched' but not shown (A1, A2).
All accounts are copies or condensations of one Vicksburg wire dispatch with no particulars of the hanging; no local, independent or follow-up report was found (A1, A2, A3, A4, A5).
